Release notes#

Status: final — published 2026-10-02

Faber 1.12 adds text processing and a cleaner set of operators to the language, and it changes what generated code looks like. Since 1.11.0 (1 October 2026) the language gained regular-expression operations (find, find_all, split, replace, escape) on a regex that is checked when it is built, the membership glyphs ∈ and ∉, and a set of settled numeric and loop rules: width limits apply only at the store for wrapping<W> too, a range step is a positive stride, and a tensor bracket read is a plain T. Four experimental code-generation targets (BASIC, Pascal, COBOL, Fortran) ship, default-off. Generated Rust, Go and TypeScript now import a named runtime package instead of carrying helper code in every file. Several of these are breaking changes; read "Breaking changes" before you upgrade a package or regenerate code.

Language#

Regex operations. A regex built with ↦ regex now supports the operations a text-processing program needs. The dialect is RE2: leftmost-first matching, linear-time where the target's engine allows it, no lookaround, no backreferences. A pattern that uses a rejected construct fails the conversion with a diagnostic that names the construct.

  • r.matches(text) is the existing boolean test.
  • r.find(text) returns match ∪ none: the leftmost match, or none.
  • r.find_all(text) returns every non-overlapping match as a list.
  • r.split(text) returns the pieces between matches. Capture groups are not spliced into the result, and leading and trailing empty pieces are kept.
  • r.replace(text, with) replaces every match. with is either a text, taken literally ($1, ${name} and \1 are plain text), or a closure from the match to a text: r.replace(text, _ m ∴ m.text().uppercase()).
  • text.escape() returns a pattern text that matches the text literally.
  • A match is read with text(), start(), end(), group(n) and named(name). Offsets are code points, half-open, never bytes. group(0) is the whole match; a group that did not take part, an index past the last group, and an unknown name are all none. The match has no source-level type name: hold it in an inferred binding (const _ m ← …) or take it as an inferred closure parameter.
  • Latin spellings are consentit, inventa, collecta, divide, muta, inventum, principium, terminus, coetus, nominatus and munita.

↦ regex is failable: it fails when the pattern does not compile, through the ordinary ⇥ string channel, and the 1.11 handling rules apply (a ⊥ default, an enclosing do { } catch, trap { }, or a function declaring ⇥ E; main is exempt). The old 1024-byte literal-pattern cap is gone.

Each target uses its own native regex engine; Faber does not ship a matcher. Where an engine cannot express a construct, the target reports it by name rather than approximating. Support: the MIR runner, Rust (faber::regex), Go (regexp), TypeScript (RegExp, through @faber/runtime/regex), Swift (Regex), Python (re), LLVM and WebAssembly (through host rows) run every operation. The Racket (sexp) target names the whole family unsupported (regex_engine_diverges), and the Haskell target fails every regex construct (regex_engine_unavailable). The named gaps are listed under "Known issues".

Membership glyphs. x ∈ xs tests membership and x ∉ xs negates it. The right operand is a list, a set, a map (the test is on the keys), an enum value set (c ∈ [Color.rubrum, Color.viridis]), or a range (age ∈ 18‥65). The keyword forms between and within (Latin between and within) are retired: they now draw PARSE001 membership_keyword_retired, which names the glyph to write. Membership never applies to text: "a" ∈ "abc" is SEM010 membership_over_text, and a substring test is haystack.contains(needle). A scalar, nullable or unresolved right operand is also rejected by name.

Numbers: width limits apply only at the store, wrapping included. wrapping<W> now follows the rule trapping and saturating already followed. An expression over wrapping operands is computed exactly and reduced only where the value is stored into a cell. With wrapping<u8> values 200 and 100, (a + b) / 2 is 150 and print a + b prints 300; the sum wraps to 44 only if it is stored into a wrapping<u8> cell. Chains of +, -, *, shifts, bit operators and unary minus that feed a wrapping store may still be reduced step by step, because that cannot be observed. The MIR runner and the Python target follow the rule; see Known issues for TypeScript.

Literals beside policy cells. An untyped constant adopts the cell type under ≡ and ≠ next to a saturating or wrapping integer cell and next to a saturating or trapping float cell, as it already did next to a bare width: saturating<u8> ≡ 250 now checks. A typed operand of another type still needs ↦, and the diagnostic text now names ≅ and ↦.

Integer to `f32` rounds once. int ↦ f32 on the MIR runner rounds directly from the integer instead of through f64.

Ranges. A range step is a positive stride and the direction comes only from the bounds: 10‥0 step 2 yields 10 8 6 4 2 and 0‥10 step 2 yields 0 2 4 6 8 (Latin step). A literal zero or negative step is the new compile error SEM011 range_step_not_positive; a computed one traps at run time. A var range binder is a fresh copy at the top of each iteration, so writing to it no longer steers the loop. Rust, Go, TypeScript and Swift emission follow the same rules.

`copy`. copy marks how a binding is initialized: var copy Point b ← a duplicates a at the declaration, and a later b ← c of a class value assigns by reference like any class assignment. After a copy parameter makes its duplicate, the callee mutates it only as far as the ordinary const / var declaration allows, and a field write and a mutating method call follow one rule: a method that changes its receiver in place (directly, through a sibling method, or through an in-place verb on a field), called on a const binding or on a parameter that is not mut, is SEM020 (imperativus_operator_method_requires_varia_receiver), exactly as a field write would be. A copy tensor binding or parameter keeps element writes and arithmetic, and a rank-2 copy tensor reads by t[[r, c]].

`mut` parameters. A mut scalar parameter requires an argument of exactly its type: passing a u8 variable to a mut int parameter is SEM010 mut_argument_type_mismatch (a store through the parameter lands in the caller's cell, so a narrower cell could otherwise hold a value it cannot). Assigning from one mut scalar parameter to another copies the value and creates no borrow, so swapping two mut int parameters through a held const no longer trips SEM052; real aliasing such as swap(x, x) still does.

Tensors and vectors. A tensor bracket read t[i] (and t[[r, c]]) is T and traps on a bad index, like a list index; a literal index provably out of bounds stays a compile error. The get / accipe method form is the nullable read. A vector<T, N> indexed with a constant lane is a lane read, write and v![k] form (a constant outside the width is a compile error), and a run-time index is a checked lane select that fails like an out-of-range list index.

Fixes to existing forms.

  • match alternatives (case A or B) now lower and run on the MIR runner; they passed faber check and then failed with an unsupported-lowering error.
  • A repeated numeric or text switch case value is SEM042 duplicate_literal naming the value, instead of an invalid-MIR failure at run time.
  • assert cond "msg" on one line is PARSE001 adfirma_message_particle (the message was silently dropped); write assert cond panic "msg". A string on the next line is still its own statement.
  • A payload-free enum no longer draws WARN025 (union_no_common_members); an enum is not a written union.
  • reduce (Latin reduce) folds into a fresh accumulator, so the caller's initial value is no longer overwritten by the result.
  • An enum variant stored into a T ∪ none slot or an optional class field, and a payload variant of a generic union (Opt<int>), now check, lower and run on the runner.
  • A declared enum annotation no longer draws the union guardrail warning.
  • The MIR runner grows its native stack per call and stops a runaway recursion at a depth of 10,000 calls with the named failure runner_call_depth_exceeded instead of aborting the process. The runner gained the stacker dependency for this.
  • faber hir lexes under the file's frontmatter locale and resolves imports like faber check; an English-locale file or a file importing a library type no longer fails under hir.
  • Swift emits postfix ! for the explicit non-null assertion.
  • The six long-retired words positivum, negativum, nonnihil, nonnulla, prae and sic are no longer reserved: they are ordinary identifiers. A use of sic as the old conditional is still recognized and draws conditional_sic_removed; that migration diagnostic and the retired-membership one are scheduled for deletion at the Faber 2 cut.

Experimental targets#

Four new code-generation targets ship as default-off Cargo features outside the default build. Each emits a fail-closed subset: a Faber feature is supported only where it maps directly onto a native construct of the target; anything that would need emulation or a runtime library is rejected by name (unsupported on target <name>: <construct>), and an emitted program prints what faber run prints.

TargetSourceOutputTool that runs it
basicMIRline-numbered BASIC listing (C64 BASIC V2 compatible)cbmbasic
pascal (alias pas)HIRFree Pascal programfpc
cobol (alias cob)HIRGnuCOBOL 3.2 free-format sourcecobc
fortran (alias f90)HIRFortran 2008 free-form sourcegfortran

On a default build faber targets lists all four with available=no, and faber emit -t <name> fails with target_unavailable naming the feature to enable (mir-basic, hir-pascal, hir-cobol, hir-fortran). Emitting needs no external tool; the tools above are only for running or checking the emitted program. The four targets are emit only (no run or package), and they are outside the ordinary scripta/e2e fleet. Each supports a small subset: integers and floats of the widths it can represent exactly, control flow, text, enums, simple records, and rank-1 and rank-2 tensors, with copy bindings of records and tensors on the targets that can copy. None supports collections, closures, the error channel, async, or the numeric policy words beyond what its README lists.

Targets#

Runtime packages (breaking for generated code). Generated Rust, Go and TypeScript no longer carry per-file helper code (exact-integer arithmetic, decimals, inf, the ¶ formatter, display helpers, generators, tensor and vector carriers). They import a runtime package, spelled by one rule per target from one table:

  • Rust: the faber crate's namespaces faber::exact, faber::inf, faber::dec, faber::format, faber::display, faber::r#gen, faber::float, plus faber::regex and faber::Match. faber::exact::store takes two arguments, the three transitional display root aliases are removed, and faber::Regex::new returns a Result. The async cursor carriers and block_on live in the crate; an optional, non-default tokio feature adds a tokio block_on. The regex feature is on by default.
  • Go: one flat rt package (import path faber/rt), spelled rt.<Namespace><Name>: for example rt.ExactStore, rt.InfI, rt.DecAdd, rt.FormatInt, rt.TensorTensor, rt.VectorVector, rt.RegexRegex and rt.SermoConversation. rt.Verum, rt.ListDisplay and rt.ValorDisplay are removed (rt.DisplayVerum, rt.DisplayList, rt.DisplayValor).
  • TypeScript: import { display, exact, dec, inf, format } from "@faber/runtime" (only the namespaces a file uses), and import * as regex from "@faber/runtime/regex". A TypeScript file that uses no runtime namespace has no import and is emitted as a script; a script that declares top-level names gets an export {}; marker so its names stay out of the global scope.

Regenerate any generated code you keep; output from 1.11 and earlier does not compile against the new runtimes, and the new output does not compile without them. Generated Rust that uses exact integers, decimals, inf, display or the formatter needs the faber crate as a dependency (it can no longer be built with bare rustc as a single file).

Readability. Generated code reads closer to hand-written code.

  • Rust: a function-tail match writes expression arms, a sole-print arm and a bound-cursor loop body drop their redundant block, a do / catch body drops its dead one-shot loop and let ok rebinding, and compiler temporaries follow one naming scheme.
  • Go: a statement if drops an else after a terminating arm, a match arm body writes no redundant block, an empty class is struct{}, an enum type switch drops any(), the do wrapper drops its dead one-shot loop, and temporaries follow one naming scheme. The Go runtime is flat, as above.
  • TypeScript: no dead trailing return after an exiting body, and temporaries follow one naming scheme.

Other target changes.

  • LLVM and WebAssembly hosts spell the regex operations through versioned rows: __faber_rt_v1_regex_* for the regex value, __faber_rt_v1_text_escape for text.escape() and __faber_rt_v1_match_* for the match accessors. The ABI spelling is __faber_rt_v1_<family>_<op>, named for the receiver family.
  • A vector lane read runs on the runner, Rust, LLVM, Racket and TypeScript; WebAssembly refuses it by name (no vector carrier), and Go and Swift carry named gaps.
  • Swift map-key and literal-key membership emit the native test, and Python follows the store-only wrapping rule.

Tooling#

  • faber explain --json carries each exemplum's grammar production ids, and faber explain --list --json emits the index as records.
  • faber check, check-library and the package build now share one manifest target resolver. An unreadable or unsupported build.target fails closed instead of falling back silently, so a build.kind = "lib" package no longer checks clean and then fails to build.
  • The package builder's path-override probe now requires the Faber runtime checkout, so a release runner with only the hosts checkout resolves the tag pin instead of a dead path.
  • faber format, convert and the codemods stay report-only by default (--write applies), as in 1.11.

GPU#

This release makes no GPU product claim. No Faber program drives the GPU through faber run, and the GPU campaign remains paused. The language-level work from 1.11 is unchanged; the vector lane read above is a language and runner feature.

Breaking changes#

  1. `↦ regex` is failable. A string ↦ regex (or ascii ↦ regex) outside main needs a handler: give it a ⊥ default, wrap it in do { } catch or trap { }, or declare ⇥ string on the function. In Rust, faber::Regex::new returns Result<Regex, RegexError>; there is no infallible alias.
  2. `between` / `within` (Latin `between` / `within`) are retired. Write x ∈ xs, x ∈ a‥b, and x ∉ … for the negation. Membership over text is rejected; use .contains(…).
  3. `wrapping<W>` reduces only at the store. An unstored expression over wrapping operands (a division, remainder, comparison, print, or ↦) is now computed exactly instead of wrapping first. To keep the wrapped value, store the expression into a wrapping<W> cell and use the cell.
  4. Range `step` is a positive stride. Rewrite step -1 to step 1 on a descending range (10‥0 step 1); a zero or negative step is SEM011 range_step_not_positive. A var range binder is a per-iteration copy and no longer steers the loop.
  5. A tensor bracket read is `T`. t[i] coalesce 0.0 and t[i] coalesce 0.0 no longer have a nullable operand: write t[i] for a trapping read, or t.get([i]) coalesce 0.0 (Latin accipe) for a nullable one.
  6. A mutating method call needs a `var` receiver. Calling a user method that changes self on a const binding or on a parameter that is not mut (copy parameters included) is SEM020; bind the value to a var local first.
  7. A `mut` scalar parameter needs an argument of exactly its type (SEM010 mut_argument_type_mismatch): convert the argument with ↦ first.
  8. A repeated switch case value is a check error (SEM042); previously it failed at run time.
  9. `assert cond "msg"` on one line is a parse error; write assert cond panic "msg".
  10. Regenerate generated code. Rust, Go and TypeScript output now imports the runtime packages (see Targets); older output and older runtimes do not match. Hand-written code that called the removed Rust and Go spellings (faber::exact::store with three arguments, the display root aliases, rt.Verum, rt.ListDisplay, rt.ValorDisplay) must use the namespaced names.
  11. LLVM and WebAssembly host authors: the regex and match rows are __faber_rt_v1_regex_*, __faber_rt_v1_text_escape and __faber_rt_v1_match_*; the host-side display helpers moved to faber::display::*.

Known issues#

  • TypeScript and `wrapping<W>`. The TypeScript emitter still reduces a wrapping<W> expression per operation, so an unstored expression differs from the runner. The wrapping<u64> corpus program fails tsc (a bigint compared with a number).
  • Regex gaps by target. Each is the target's own engine, recorded rather than emulated:
  • Go has no Unicode \b: a pattern with \b or \B fails the conversion on Go with unicode_word_boundary.
  • TypeScript clears a repeated group's captures at every iteration, so ((a)|b)* over range reads group 2 as none; no diagnostic is issued.
  • Swift differs from the dialect on (?m) with CR and U+2028 line ends, on \b next to combining marks and digits, and on (?i) folding of a few letters (σ / ς).
  • Python rejects script and binary-property classes (\p{Greek}, \p{Alphabetic}) with unicode_property, and rebinds a nullable repeated group's capture to the empty text.
  • The linear-time guarantee holds on Rust, Go, LLVM and WebAssembly. TypeScript, Python and Swift use backtracking engines, so a pattern such as ^(a+)+$ can take exponential time there.
  • Unicode property classes follow each engine's Unicode version.
  • On WebAssembly, a do { } catch around ↦ regex, the char carrier and a template with more than three operands are unsupported (try_call, char and text format arity diagnostics); no Wasm host ships, so Wasm run tiers are unmeasured.
  • Racket (sexp) and Haskell name every regex construct unsupported.
  • Range containment `∈ a‥b` / `∉ a‥b` has no MIR lowering: it does not run on the MIR runner, Racket, LLVM or WebAssembly. The HIR targets emit it.
  • Rust half-width float cells. trapping<f16>, saturating<f16>, the bf16 forms and bare f16 / bf16 emit through faber emit --target rust, exit 0, and then fail at rustc.
  • Rust corpus builds. Two corpus programs still fail to build on Rust (one stores an awaited promise at a ← binding, one converts composite values behind a value).
  • Print and templates.
  • print a, b lays out one value per line on the MIR text targets (runner and Racket) when an argument is a sized integer, enum, class, union, d64, inf or tensor, and the first argument is not a literal; the other targets join with spaces. The layout also depends on the argument count. The comma form is under review for removal; prefer a string template, print "§ §"(a, b), which joins uniformly.
  • LLVM has no template format rows for sized integers (i8, i16, i32, u8, u16, u32), enums and several composites, and print of an i16 does not link; a u64 above the i64 maximum prints signed in a template.
  • Haskell rejects every string template, and a program with two or more output statements runs only the last.
  • These gaps were measured on the 2 October tree.
  • `print` tokens are Latin in every locale. Booleans, none and the tuple head print as true / false / none / tuple even in an English file. The ruling is that they follow the code locale (true / false / none / tuple); the change is not made yet.
  • Enum and union residuals. The Racket target prints a map holding an enum or generic union variant as a raw hash; Go fails to compile a generic unit variant; Python and Swift reject generic enums and maps.
  • Other open defects. cumulate (Latin cumulata) folds into the caller's own accumulator the way reduce used to. The checker accepts narrowing an inferred error result with is and ✓ ✗ without an explicit T ∪ E annotation, and only MIR validation rejects it. int ↦ f32 still rounds twice on Python, and WebAssembly types the local as f64. faber convert does not resolve imports (a file that imports a library type fails with SEM002).
  • WebAssembly. Programs that use a list are refused by the Wasm emitter (BoundedArray unsupported); carried from 1.11.
  • Experimental targets differ from `faber run` where the target's arithmetic does. COBOL checks only stored values, Pascal traps per operation at its own native 64-bit limit (run-time error 215) where the runner checks at the store, and BASIC numbers are the C64 40-bit float. Targets that print a boolean print true / false. Each target rejects the cases it cannot match by name.
  • Library and gate status. No gate runs the Gradus library's test suites, and several remain red or blocked; Tela's concatenating gates were red before the TypeScript runtime change and have not been re-run on this tree.
  • Public compatibility matrices. The measurement data and the rendered matrices in the public Faber repository are regenerated for this release (the keyword rows within and between are gone).
  • Per-target conformance gaps against the 601-program corpus, measured on the release tree: Go has 14 unexpected failures (ceiling 31 expected), Swift 17, TypeScript 5 (plus 4 recorded gaps that now pass), Racket (sexp) 5, the Faber re-emit round trip 8 files, and Wasm 17 per-program tier regressions. LLVM refuses 59 programs with a named diagnostic. The MIR runner passes 428 programs end to end; Rust passes 492. The Swift float-cell exemplum stays a Swift expected failure because it also uses inf.
  • Carried from 1.10: the Gather reverse-mode check, environment-gated device checks, and package checks that need the optional Triga provider.

Not in this release#

  • Multi-subject match a and b is not checked or lowered; do not rely on it.
  • Character ranges as set bounds (x ∈ '0'…'9') are not supported; interval bounds are numbers. Text membership stays .contains.
  • The slash regex literal and per-group spans are not shipped; read group spans from the match with start() and group(n).
  • Collection-ergonomics rewrite, set-algebra glyphs, superscript powers, reduce / thread kernel forms, and do all remain planned.
  • externa typing and conditional-compilation enforcement stay held; there is no LSP.
  • Translated reader packs (ar, hi, th-TH, vi, zh-Hans, zh-Hant) keep their own spelling for the null type until the word is chosen.
  • A print display-locale change (Latin tokens to the code locale), and removal of the comma print form, are decided in direction only.
  • Public publication of the Go runtime module and @faber/runtime waits for the Faber 2 migration; they are consumed by path here.
  • No GPU program runs through faber run.
  • Cista stays on the 0.1.0 line; Radix stays at 0.84.0 (no separate Radix release).

Candidate evidence (operator record)#

This section records the local gates run on the candidate tree. It is for the operator and is omitted from public rendering. Paths are relative; the lane is a worktree packet (own target/) on an 18-core Mac. Gate results quote the run as it happened. Commands that call rm (the release scripts' cleanup) ran with a no-op rm shim on PATH.

Pins. Radix source commit the candidate is cut from: 6d10e722e (main when the lane was created), plus one bump commit (26026812e), one pack-digest commit (f25c317bc) and this notes commit. Hosts pin moved e755e5c969fe to 3002760912f3 (the packet sibling; manifest and the build-stamped HOSTS_PINNED_REV agree). Public Faber target API: faberlang/faber main with the matrices commit e812b44 (v1.12.0 is the tag the generated manifests resolve; the tag does not exist yet, which verify-dev-kit reports as its one RESIDUAL). It carries the new runtime namespaces (faber::exact, inf, dec, format, display, gen, float, regex), which v1.11.0 does not. Radix crate version stays 0.84.0; the faber crate is 1.12.0.

Runbook local proof. validate-release-manifest ok; faber-regen-lock --pinned-siblings --check ok (hosts pin match, lock fresh); cargo build --locked --release -p faber --bin faber ok (48 s cold); release-gate recipe (remapped, --locked --release) ok (47 s); faber --version prints faber 1.12.0; scan-release-leakage clean (0 workspace paths, 0 registry paths); assemble-dev-kit ok; verify-dev-kit PASSED (all positives and negatives; one RESIDUAL: the D1 git-dependency build needs the faber tag, and the emitted form is faber = { package = "faber", git = "https://github.com/faberlang/faber", tag = "v1.12.0" }); package-archive ok; smoke-test-release-archive RELEASABLE. Local archive faber-v1.12.0-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz; launcher digest 376b9f47…e76af (reproduced identically on a second assemble from the final candidate), and reference-pack digest a00e996d…cc4c; both are recorded in the manifest. The reference-pack digest depends on the commit stamped into PACK.toml, so it is the digest at the manifest's radix pin (6d10e722e); a later commit changes it. CI rebuilds the launcher, so its digest may differ.

`release-gate --locked-release-build` (run once on the candidate, 57 s): locked release build ok, leakage scan clean, cargo test -p faber --test hygiene 1 passed, cargo test -p faber 1182 passed, 0 failed, 23 ignored; === release-gate · ok ===.

Ladder. Stage 1 ok (18 s, fmt clean, all 53 workspace members checked). Stage 2 ok (15 s, 0 errors). Stage 3 ok (1 canary package, 2 s). Stage 4a ok (82 s: reader pack, compat measurement fresh, MIR and HIR coverage). Stage 4b ok (979 s; over the 548 s of 1.11.0, a slow-gate finding): `genuine FAILs 0 across 0 crate(s)`, 53 crates ok. Stage 4c ok (107 s). Stage 4d ok (9 s, Metal spike on Apple M5 Max). Stage 4e ok (6 s). Stage 5 ok (18 s, no grammar disagreement outside the baseline).

E2E (one lane at a time). runner ok (428/601 pass, 368/368 pinned goldens; 25 s). Rust ok (492/601 pass, 599/601 accepted, 2 ledger-known build failures, await-assignment and valor-composita-deep; 293 s). canonical RED (the same two miscompiling members). Go: emit stage unexpected (defectus, async_generator); golden 407/601 pass, 587/601 accepted, 14 unexpected, expected failures 31 at ceiling

  1. TypeScript: lint 3 unexpected; golden 188/193 expected outcomes accepted, 5 unexpected, 4 stale. Swift: emit stage red; golden 584/601 accepted, 253 run, 17 unexpected. Wasm: parse, emit, lint, build ok; golden RED (17 tier regressions, 322/601 emitted, 0 runnable: no stub host ships). Public matrices. scripta/emit-compat-json.py regenerated nothing new (the committed measurement is current). render-matrices.py --check was stale and was re-rendered in the faber repo (e812b44, with the README support percentages).

Operator steps the runbook requires. (1) Push faberlang/hosts main (the manifest hosts pin must exist on the remote) and faberlang/faber main. (2) Tag faberlang/faber v1.12.0 at e812b44. (3) Merge the release branch to Radix main, then tag faber/v1.12.0 on the release commit and push it to start the release workflow. (4) After the workflow, verify downloaded archives by checksum and smoke before promotion. Known-red items above need the operator's acknowledgement, per the release protocol.
